sentenceSets.sentence: The publisher expurgated the correspondence before releasing it, removing passages that might have embarrassed living figures.

answerChoices.reasoning: Abridging shortens a text for convenience, but the cuts here were chosen by what might embarrass particular people who are still alive.
Annotating adds explanatory notes, whereas the sentence describes material being taken out before publication.
Redacting blacks out passages so the reader can see that something was withheld, while this publisher released a version from which the embarrassing matter had been quietly removed.
Paraphrasing keeps the content while changing the words, which would not protect anyone from the embarrassment the passages contain.
Authentication establishes that the letters are genuine, a separate matter from what the publisher chose to cut.
Cataloguing organizes the letters for reference and involves removing nothing from them.
Serializing releases material in installments, which is a matter of publishing schedule rather than of excising passages.
Translation changes the language of the correspondence and would leave the awkward passages fully intact.
Restoring would put missing material back, the opposite of removing passages before release.
Fabricating would mean inventing letters, whereas the publisher is described as cutting from existing ones.
Publicizing draws attention to the material, which works against the aim of sparing living figures embarrassment.

sentenceSets.sentence: School boards in three counties voted to expurgate the anthology, and teachers arrived in September to find four poems missing.

answerChoices.reasoning: A ban would keep the whole anthology out of classrooms, but the teachers still have the book and find only four poems gone from it.
Reprinting is a manufacturing decision that would not by itself explain particular poems disappearing from the collection.
Replacing the anthology would put a different book in teachers' hands, whereas they received the same one with gaps in it.
Reviewing the anthology would be an assessment, and the sentence reports an action whose immediate result is missing poems.
Endorsement approves a text as it stands and cannot account for four poems being gone.
Purchasing copies would supply the anthology intact rather than shortened by four poems.
Digitizing changes the format and would preserve the contents rather than thin them.
Translation would alter the language of the poems, not remove them from the volume.
Expanding the anthology would add poems, contradicting the four that are missing.
Memorizing is something students do and is not a decision a school board takes by vote.
Praise leaves the contents untouched and explains nothing about the gaps teachers discovered.

sentenceSets.sentence: Late in life he tried to expurgate his own diaries, but the ink he used to blot the worst entries proved disappointingly transparent.

answerChoices.reasoning: Concealing would mean hiding the diaries away whole, but he is working inside them entry by entry to get rid of what he now regrets.
Destroying the diaries would leave nothing behind, whereas he keeps the volumes and works only on the worst entries within them.
Revising implies rewriting toward a better version, while his ink is applied to blot out passages rather than to improve them.
Publishing would expose the entries, the reverse of an effort undone by ink that failed to hide them.
Indexing would help a reader find entries, which is the last thing someone blotting them would want.
Dating entries is a clerical act and has nothing to do with covering over compromising passages.
Binding concerns the physical assembly of the volumes rather than the content of particular entries.
Bequeathing the diaries would pass them to someone else intact, which his blotting was meant to prevent.
Recopying would reproduce the very entries he is trying to blot out.
Advertising the diaries would call attention to the material he was struggling to obscure.
Making the entries more legible runs directly against ink applied to cover them.
